items.question_text: A 58-year-old man has a positive faecal immunochemical test. He has read that the test is 70% sensitive and asks what his chance of cancer is. You cannot quote his personal chance from sensitivity alone. What is the most appropriate explanation?
options: His chance of cancer cannot be stated from sensitivity and specificity alone
His chance of cancer is 95%
His chance of cancer is 90%
A positive test in a sensitive assay means the disease is present
Specificity of 90% means 90% of positive tests are true
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. His chance of cancer cannot be stated from sensitivity and specificity alone

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A 58-year-old man has a positive faecal immunochemical test. He has read that the test is 70% sensitive and asks what his chance of cancer is. You cannot quote his personal chance from sensitivity alone.

2. THE RULE
Sensitivity and specificity are test properties; a negative highly sensitive test helps rule disease out, and the post-test probability also needs prevalence or likelihood ratios.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Sensitivity is the proportion of people with disease who test positive. Specificity is the proportion without disease who test negative. Neither is the positive predictive value. PPV needs prevalence as well.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. His chance of cancer is 95%: That is the sensitivity, not his post-test probability.
C. His chance of cancer is 90%: That is the specificity.
D. A positive test in a sensitive assay means the disease is present: A sensitive test still has false positives.
E. Specificity of 90% means 90% of positive tests are true: That confuses specificity with PPV.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Sensitivity and specificity are test properties; a negative highly sensitive test helps rule disease out, and the post-test probability also needs prevalence or likelihood ratios.

---

items.question_text: A screening test is used in two towns. The test is identical. A student says the positive predictive value must be the same because the test has not changed. What is the most appropriate statement?
options: PPV is the same. The test characteristics are unchanged
PPV is higher where prevalence is higher
PPV is higher in the university clinic because the students are healthier
PPV equals specificity in both clinics
Sensitivity falls when prevalence falls
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. PPV is higher where prevalence is higher

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
The same test has a lower positive predictive value in the low-prevalence clinic.

2. THE RULE
Positive predictive value rises and falls with prevalence even when sensitivity and specificity are fixed, and a positive screening test still needs diagnostic confirmation.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
PPV is true positives divided by all positives. At low prevalence most positives are false positives, so PPV falls. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test. PPV is a property of the test in a population.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. PPV is the same. The test characteristics are unchanged: Sensitivity and specificity are unchanged. PPV is not.
C. PPV is higher in the university clinic because the students are healthier: Lower prevalence lowers PPV.
D. PPV equals specificity in both clinics: They are different quantities.
E. Sensitivity falls when prevalence falls: Sensitivity does not.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
PPV rises with prevalence.

---

A negative result on a sensitive test helps rule disease out
A positive D-dimer in low-risk patients confirms embolism
D-dimer sensitivity is irrelevant to a rule-out pathway

CORRECT ANSWER

C. A negative result on a sensitive test helps rule disease out

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A negative sensitive test helps rule disease out. Specificity is not the property that does that job.

2. THE RULE
Sensitivity and specificity are test properties; a negative highly sensitive test helps rule disease out, and the post-test probability also needs prevalence or likelihood ratios.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
A highly sensitive test, when negative, makes the disease unlikely. That is the rule-out use. A highly specific test, when positive, helps rule in. D-dimer is used as a sensitive rule-out test in low-risk patients, not as a rule-in test.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG

B. Specificity is the chance the patient has the disease: Specificity is a test property, not a post-test probability.
D. A positive D-dimer in low-risk patients confirms embolism: D-dimer has many false positives.
E. D-dimer sensitivity is irrelevant to a rule-out pathway: Sensitivity is why the pathway works.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
SnNOut: a sensitive test, if negative, helps rule out.

items.question_text: A registrar confuses two figures in a report. One is the number of new cases of a disease in a year. The other is the number of people who currently have it. What is the most appropriate distinction?
options: Incidence counts existing cases. Prevalence counts new cases
Prevalence always falls when incidence is stable
Incidence includes deaths. Prevalence does not
Incidence is new cases in a period. Prevalence is existing cases at a time
They are interchangeable in chronic disease
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Incidence is new cases in a period. Prevalence is existing cases at a time

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Incidence is new cases. Prevalence is existing cases. A stable incidence can still raise prevalence.

2. THE RULE
Incidence is new cases in a population over a period of time, while prevalence is all existing cases at a point in time.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Incidence is the rate of new cases. Prevalence is the proportion who have the disease at a point. Prevalence can rise if people live longer with the disease, even when incidence is flat.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Incidence counts existing cases. Prevalence counts new cases: That reverses the definitions.
B. Prevalence always falls when incidence is stable: Longer survival raises prevalence.
C. Incidence includes deaths. Prevalence does not: Deaths remove people from the prevalent pool.
E. They are interchangeable in chronic disease: The distinction matters more in chronic disease, not less.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Incidence is new cases over time.

---

items.question_text: A trial reports that a treatment reduces the absolute risk of an outcome from 8% to 4%. A student asks for the number needed to treat. What is the number needed to treat?
options: NNT is 4
NNT is 40
NNT is 10
NNT cannot be calculated without the p-value
NNT is 25
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. NNT is 25

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Absolute reduction is 4 percentage points. NNT is 25, not 4.

2. THE RULE
The number needed to treat is 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction, and relative risk reductions overstate small absolute benefits.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
Absolute risk reduction is 10% minus 6%, which is 4 percentage points, or 0.04. NNT is 1 / 0.04 = 25. The 40% figure is the relative risk reduction and is not the NNT.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. NNT is 4: That treats the relative reduction as if it were the absolute one.
B. NNT is 40: That is the relative reduction written as a whole number.
C. NNT is 10: That is the placebo event rate, not the difference.
D. NNT cannot be calculated without the p-value: NNT is an effect size. The p-value is a separate question.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction.

---

items.question_text: A newspaper says a drug halves the risk of a rare event. The event fell from 2 per 1000 to 1 per 1000. A patient asks if that means half of people are saved. What is the most appropriate explanation?

Half of vaccinated people avoid the outcome

CORRECT ANSWER

A. The absolute reduction is 1 per 1000. The 50% figure is relative

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
The 50% is relative. The absolute reduction is 1 event per 1000 people.

2. THE RULE
The number needed to treat is 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction, and relative risk reductions overstate small absolute benefits.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Relative risk reduction is (2 − 1) / 2 = 50%. Absolute risk reduction is 1 per 1000. The advertisement uses the relative figure. The absolute figure is what tells the patient how many events are prevented.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Half of vaccinated people avoid the outcome: That misreads a relative reduction as a personal probability.
C. The absolute reduction is 50%: 50% is the relative figure.
D. Relative risk reduction cannot exceed absolute risk reduction: Relative often exceeds absolute when the baseline is small.
E. The trial shows no effect because the rates are both small: Small rates can still have a real relative effect.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Always pair a relative reduction with the absolute one.

items.question_text: A trial reports a relative risk of 0.8 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.5 to 1.3. A colleague says the treatment works because the point estimate is under 1. Statistical significance is not shown. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The result is statistically significant because 0.80 is below 1
The interval includes 1, so a null effect is not excluded
The treatment is proven harmful
The p-value must be below 0.05 because the point estimate moved
A confidence interval is the range of individual patient results
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. The interval includes 1, so a null effect is not excluded

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
The interval crosses 1. The point estimate of 0.80 does not prove an effect.

2. THE RULE
A 95% confidence interval that includes the null value is compatible with no effect, and a non-significant result in a small study may be a type II error.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
A 95% confidence interval that includes the null value, here a relative risk of 1, does not exclude no effect. The point estimate of 0.80 is the best single guess. It is not proof.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. The result is statistically significant because 0.80 is below 1: Significance is about the interval or the p-value, not the direction of the point estimate alone.
C. The treatment is proven harmful: The interval also includes benefit.
D. The p-value must be below 0.05 because the point estimate moved: An interval crossing 1 corresponds to a p-value above 0.05.
E. A confidence interval is the range of individual patient results: It is an interval for the estimated effect, not for individual outcomes.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
An interval that includes the null does not exclude no effect.

---

items.question_text: A paper reports p = 0.03 for a difference. A student says this means there is a 3% chance the result is due to chance, or a 97% chance the treatment works. What is the most appropriate explanation?
options: p = 0.03 is the probability the null is true
p = 0.03 proves the effect is clinically important
p = 0.03 is the probability of a result at least this extreme if the null were true
p = 0.03 means the drug works in 97% of patients
A p-value below 0.05 means the study was adequately powered
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. p = 0.03 is the probability of a result at least this extreme if the null were true

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
p = 0.03 is not a 3% chance that the drug does not work.

2. THE RULE
A 95% confidence interval that includes the null value is compatible with no effect, and a non-significant result in a small study may be a type II error.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
The p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as those observed, assuming the null is true. It is not the probability that the null is true, and it is not a measure of clinical importance.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. p = 0.03 is the probability the null is true: That is the common misreading.
B. p = 0.03 proves the effect is clinically important: Statistical significance is not clinical importance.
D. p = 0.03 means the drug works in 97% of patients: That confuses a p-value with a response rate.
E. A p-value below 0.05 means the study was adequately powered: Power is set before the study. A small p-value does not prove it.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
A p-value assumes the null and describes the data.

---

items.question_text: A screening program reports longer survival from diagnosis in screened patients than in unscreened patients. A colleague says this proves the program reduces deaths. What is the most appropriate caution?
options: Longer survival from diagnosis proves a mortality benefit
This is length-time bias
Screening always reduces mortality if survival from diagnosis rises
Earlier diagnosis can lengthen survival time without delaying death
Lead time applies only to infectious disease
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Earlier diagnosis can lengthen survival time without delaying death

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Longer survival from diagnosis is not proof of benefit. The diagnosis may simply have been made earlier.

2. THE RULE
Lead-time and length-time biases can make screening look beneficial for survival without delaying death.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Lead time is the interval between screen detection and the time the disease would have presented clinically. Survival measured from diagnosis lengthens by that interval even if the date of death is unchanged.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Longer survival from diagnosis proves a mortality benefit: The clock started earlier.
B. This is length-time bias: Length-time bias is the tendency of screening to find slower-growing disease.
C. Screening always reduces mortality if survival from diagnosis rises: That is the biased reading.
E. Lead time applies only to infectious disease: It is a screening concept.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Lead-time bias shifts the start of the survival clock.

---

items.question_text: In a randomised trial, some patients allocated to treatment did not take it, and some allocated to control obtained it elsewhere. A student wants to analyse only those who took the treatment. It preserves the randomisation. What is the most appropriate analysis?
options: Analyse by allocated group. That is the intention-to-treat estimate
Analyse only those who received the allocated treatment. That measures efficacy
Move the crossovers into the arm they ended up in
Exclude anyone who missed a visit
Intention to treat applies only to drug trials
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Analyse by allocated group. That is the intention-to-treat estimate

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Keep people in the arm they were randomised to. Dropping crossovers breaks the protection of randomisation.

2. THE RULE
Intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in their allocated group, and allocation concealment differs from blinding.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Intention to treat keeps every randomised participant in the allocated arm. It estimates the effect of offering the treatment, preserves randomisation, and avoids bias from drop-out and crossover. A per-protocol analysis answers a different question and can mislead.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Analyse only those who received the allocated treatment. That measures efficacy: That is per-protocol. It is not the primary unbiased estimate.
C. Move the crossovers into the arm they ended up in: That is as-treated analysis and breaks randomisation.
D. Exclude anyone who missed a visit: Missingness is handled. It is not a reason to drop the principle.
E. Intention to treat applies only to drug trials: It applies to any randomised comparison.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Intention to treat follows allocation, not receipt.

---

Sealed envelopes are about concealment. Knowing the arm afterwards is a blinding issue. They are not the same failure.

Intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in their allocated group, and allocation concealment differs from blinding.

Allocation concealment stops the recruiter knowing the next assignment. Blinding stops participants or assessors knowing which arm a person is in after assignment. A surgical trial can conceal allocation and still be unblinded.

A. Concealment and blinding are the same safeguard: They act at different times.
C. Surgery trials cannot conceal allocation: They can. They often cannot blind the patient.
D. Open outcome assessment repairs a failed concealment: It does not.
E. Envelopes are a form of blinding: Envelopes, if truly opaque and sequenced, are concealment.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Concealment is before assignment.

Smoking is a plausible confounder. The coffee association is not clean.

A confounder is linked to both exposure and outcome and distorts the association, and unmeasured confounders can persist after adjustment.

B. This is lead-time bias: Lead time is about screening.
C. Randomisation has removed the problem: This was not a randomised comparison.
D. A confounder must be on the causal pathway: A factor on the pathway is a mediator, not a confounder.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
A confounder links to both exposure and outcome, and is not a mediator.

items.question_text: A test has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 80%. A student asks for the positive likelihood ratio. What is the positive likelihood ratio?

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Positive likelihood ratio is 4.5, not 0.9.

2. THE RULE
Sensitivity and specificity are test properties; a negative highly sensitive test helps rule disease out, and the post-test probability also needs prevalence or likelihood ratios.

A. 0.9: That is the sensitivity, not the ratio.
C. 1.125: That is sensitivity / specificity.
D. 0.125: That is not the positive ratio.
E. Prevalence is required before a likelihood ratio can be calculated: Likelihood ratios are independent of prevalence. Predictive values are not.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity).

items.question_text: In a cohort, the risk of the outcome is 20% in the exposed and 10% in the unexposed. A student reports an odds ratio of 2.25 and calls it the relative risk. What is the most appropriate statement?

items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Risk doubled. The odds ratio of 2.7 overstates that because the outcome is common.

2. THE RULE
When the outcome is common, the odds ratio overstates the relative risk, so cohort data should report the relative risk.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Relative risk is 0.40 / 0.20 = 2. The odds are 0.40/0.60 versus 0.20/0.80, so the odds ratio is (0.667) / (0.25) = 2.67. When the outcome is common, the odds ratio pulls away from the relative risk.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Odds ratio and relative risk are always equal: They converge only when the outcome is rare.
B. The relative risk is 2.7: That is the odds ratio.
C. A common outcome makes the odds ratio smaller than the relative risk: It makes it larger.
E. Relative risk cannot be calculated in a cohort: A cohort is where relative risk is natural.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Relative risk is the risk ratio.

items.question_text: A small trial finds no significant difference between two treatments. A colleague says this proves they are equivalent. What is the most appropriate caution?
options: They have proved equivalence

items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. A type II error is likely. Absence of a significant difference is not evidence of no difference

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Not significant in an underpowered trial is not proof of equivalence.

2. THE RULE
A 95% confidence interval that includes the null value is compatible with no effect, and a non-significant result in a small study may be a type II error.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
Power is 1 minus the type II error rate. At 40% power, a real difference of the hoped-for size will be missed often. 'Not significant' is not the same as 'no difference'.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. They have proved equivalence: Equivalence needs a pre-set margin and adequate precision.
B. The p-value must be 0.40: Power is not a p-value.
C. Power of 40% means the result is significant: Power is the chance of detecting an effect, not a result.
D. Type I error is the failure to detect a real effect: That is type II.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Type II error is missing a real effect.

---

items.question_text: A trial reports a relative risk of 0.8 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.5 to 1.3. Which of the following is most accurate?

p is not needed if the estimate is 0.8
The interval proves harm
Significance is shown

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A trial reports a relative risk of 0.8 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.5 to 1.3.

2. THE RULE
A 95% confidence interval that includes the null value is compatible with no effect, and a non-significant result in a small study may be a type II error.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Interval crosses 1. Compatible with no effect. Do not call it significant.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. The treatment works because the point estimate is under 1: The point estimate alone does not show an effect when the CI crosses 1.
C. p is not needed if the estimate is 0.8: The CI already shows a lack of significance; a point estimate is not enough.
D. The interval proves harm: The interval includes both benefit and harm and proves neither.
E. Significance is shown: A CI crossing 1 means the result is not significant at 5%.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
A 95% confidence interval that includes the null value is compatible with no effect, and a non-significant result in a small study may be a type II error.

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A cohort study reports an outcome risk of 20% in the exposed group and 10% in the unexposed group. A registrar reports the odds ratio as if it were the relative risk.

2. THE RULE
When the outcome is common, the odds ratio overstates the relative risk, so cohort data should report the relative risk.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Common outcome inflates the odds ratio relative to the risk ratio.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. The odds ratio is always smaller than the relative risk: For a harmful exposure the OR is further from 1, not smaller.
C. They never differ: They differ when the outcome is common.
D. Only case-control studies have this problem: The divergence is a property of the measures, in any design.
E. A 20% risk is rare: A 20% risk is common, not rare.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
When the outcome is common, the odds ratio overstates the relative risk, so cohort data should report the relative risk.
